Internal resistance (Rs​)

Words: 37
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An effective source resistance in a specified circuit model: a source with electromotive force E drives I=E/(Rs​+RL​) through a resistive load RL​. A biological source or electrochemical interface can require a frequency-dependent or nonlinear model instead.

Capacitor bridge with series loss and a parallel standard arm

Words: 52
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
Consider two voltage dividers across a common source, with impedances Z0​,Z1​ in one branch and R1​,Zp​ in the other. Equal midpoint voltage phasors imply Z0​Zp​=R1​Z1​. If Z0​=R0​+1/(iωC0​), Z1​=1/(iωC1​) and Zp​=(1/R+iωC)−1, then separating real and imaginary parts proves R0​=R1​C/C1​ and C0​=RC1​/R1​. The topology, especially the parallel standard arm, is essential.

Maxwell bridge

Words: 54
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A null electrical circuit for measuring a lossy inductor against a standard capacitor. If opposite arms are Rx​+iωLx​ and (1/R1​+iωC)−1, and the remaining arms are R2​,R3​, balance requires their products to agree. Consequently Rx​=R2​R3​/R1​ and Lx​=CR2​R3​. Two independent real adjustments are necessary; changing the source frequency does not change the ideal balance conditions.

Equal-ratio RC bridge (ω0−2​=Rx2​Cx​(C−Cx​))

Words: 66
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A bridge driven between top and bottom nodes has equal resistors on its left arms, upper-right electrical impedance Z=Rx​/(1+iωRx​Cx​) and lower-right electrical impedance W=Rv​+1/(iωC). A zero detector electric current requires Z=W. Equating real parts and imaginary parts gives Rv​=Rx​(1−Cx​/C) and ω0−2​=Rx2​Cx​(C−Cx​), requiring 0<Cx​<C. Its open-circuit right-minus-left junction voltage is V0​(W−Z)/[2(W+Z)], whereas a connected ideal ammeter has zero terminal voltage at every angular frequency. This distinction separates a null-current measurement from an unloaded voltage measurement.

Duty cycle (D=tactive​/tcycle​)

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
The fraction of an operating cycle spent in a specified active state. For two constant-current states, average current is Iˉ=DIa​+(1−D)Is​; wake-up transients require an additional energy term.

Duty cycling

Words: 29
Duty cycle OurBigBook.com
Alternating an active mode with a lower-power mode to reduce average demand. Sleep current and transition overhead prevent average power from falling indefinitely in direct proportion to active time.

Short circuit

Words: 47
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal short circuit fixes zero electric potential difference across a terminal pair, corresponding to zero load electrical impedance. At the end of a lossless transmission line, its voltage-wave reflection coefficient is −1 and the terminal voltage is zero. The available current is still limited by source and circuit impedances; real short circuits can dissipate substantial Joule heating.

Open circuit

Words: 40
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal open circuit permits no conduction electric current through a terminal pair, corresponding to infinite load electrical impedance. At the end of a lossless transmission line, its voltage-wave reflection coefficient is +1 and the terminal current is zero. Real open terminals may retain parasitic capacitance and radiation loss.

Virtual ground

Words: 70
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A circuit node held close to zero electric potential by active feedback, without being directly connected to the reference conductor. In an ideal linear operational amplifier with its non-inverting input grounded and stable negative feedback, V−​=V+​=0 while neither input draws electric current. External branch currents meeting the inverting node therefore obey Kirchhoff's current law without flowing into the amplifier input. Equality of the input potentials fails when the output saturates or the feedback ceases to enforce linear operation.

Wien bridge

Words: 185 Articles: 1
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An alternating-current electrical circuit comparing a parallel resistor-capacitor arm with a series resistor-capacitor arm. Let the upper-left arm have electrical impedance Z1​=R1​/(1+iωR1​C1​), the lower-left arm Z2​=R2​+1/(iωC2​), and the upper-right and lower-right arms have electrical resistances R3​,R4​. For input between the upper and lower nodes and an unloaded difference measurement between the arm junctions, voltage divider balance requires Z2​/Z1​=R4​/R3​. Separating real and imaginary parts gives
ω2R1​R2​C1​C2​=1,R3​R4​​=R1​R2​​+C2​C1​​.
(1)
The balance angular frequency is positive for positive components. Equal R1​=R2​=R and C1​=C2​=C require ω=1/(RC) and R4​=2R3​. Reversing which reactive arm is upper changes the divider ratios, so the connections must always be specified.

Wien bridge band-pass response (H=−[3+i(u−u−1)]−1)

Words: 88
Wien bridge OurBigBook.com
Use the equal-component Wien bridge with upper-left parallel arm and lower-left series arm. Let A be the left arm junction, C the upper input node, and Vi​ the upper-minus-lower input electric potential difference. With u=ωRC, the unloaded transfer ratio H=(VA​−VC​)/Vi​ is the displayed expression. Its band-pass filter magnitude is [9+(u−u−1)2]−1/2, maximal at u=1 with H=−1/3. One continuous wave phase is ϕ=−π−arctan[(u−u−1)/3], tending from −π/2 at low positive frequency to −3π/2 at high frequency. Reversing the measured output polarity multiplies H by −1 and shifts its phase by π without changing its magnitude.

Two-port network

Words: 48
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A two-port network relates voltage and current, or incoming and outgoing travelling-wave amplitudes, at two pairs of electrical terminals. Power-normalized scattering parameters obey bi​=∑j​Sij​aj​. In a reciprocal network with equal reference impedances, S12​=S21​. A load reflection at port 2 can return through both transmission coefficients to port 1.

Parallel circuit

Words: 29
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A connection in which branches share both terminal nodes and therefore the same electric potential difference. Branch electric currents add. For sinusoidal signals, the total electrical admittance is the sum of branch electrical admittances; ideal capacitances add.

LC circuit (ω0​=1/LC​)

Words: 148 Articles: 2
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal electrical circuit exchanges energy between an inductor and a capacitor. With no electrical resistance or applied drive, the electric charge obeys Lq′′+q/C=0, giving angular frequency ω0​=1/LC​. A series RLC circuit adds dissipation and can include an external drive.

Parallel LC circuit (Z=jωL/(1−ω2LC))

Words: 46
LC circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal inductor and capacitor in parallel have electrical admittance 1/Z=1/(jωL)+jωC for phasors with time dependence ejωt. The branch currents cancel at angular frequency ω0​=1/LC​, giving zero total electrical admittance and an infinite limiting electrical impedance. Below this resonance its electrical reactance is positive; above it the electrical reactance is negative. Losses make the peak finite.

Series-fed parallel LC voltage response (H(ω)={1−iR[1/(ωL)−ωC]}−1)

Words: 73
LC circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal voltage source drives a series resistor feeding a parallel inductor and capacitor. In the eiωt convention, the branch voltage ratio is the title expression. It is a band-pass response with unit peak at 1/LC​, phase from +π/2 through zero to −π/2, and half-power bandwidth 1/(RC). At resonance the input current vanishes while equal and opposite inductor/capacitor currents remain finite. Reactive branch-current magnitudes must be combined as phasors, not added as positive scalars.

Diode

Words: 3k Articles: 24
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
A diode is a two-terminal component with an asymmetric current-voltage characteristic: reversing its terminal electric potential difference need not reverse its electric current with the same magnitude. Name the terminals diode anode A and diode cathode K. Define VD​=ϕA​−ϕK​ using their electric potentials, and take positive electric current ID​ from A to K. The bar in the diode symbol marks K. Positive VD​ is the forward direction; negative VD​ is the reverse direction.[ref]
The asymmetry makes a rectifier possible: a sinusoid can drive electric current through a resistor on one half of each cycle. An ordinary resistor obeying Ohm's law instead reverses its electric current when the applied electric potential difference reverses. The useful idea is directional selection; the ideal diode model captures it, while the Shockley diode equation describes a smooth exponential function rather than an abrupt switch.

Diode anode (A)

Words: 16
Diode OurBigBook.com
The terminal of a diode at which positive forward electric current enters, with the orientation used in the ideal diode model.

Diode cathode (K)

Words: 17
Diode OurBigBook.com
The terminal of a diode at which positive forward electric current leaves. The bar in the diode symbol identifies this terminal.

Ideal diode model (ID​≥0, VD​≤0, ID​VD​=0)

Words: 122
Diode OurBigBook.com
The ideal diode model sets the conducting electric potential difference to zero and the blocking electric current to zero. With the stated orientation,
conducting:blocking:​VD​=0,ID​≥0,ID​=0,VD​≤0.​
(2)
[ref]
The surrounding electrical circuit chooses the state and remaining value. The two branches meet at VD​=ID​=0. Their product vanishes, so the ideal diode dissipates no power: PD​=VD​ID​=0.
The ideal diode model omits forward drop, reverse leakage, diode reverse breakdown and switching delay.

Shockley diode equation (ID​=IS​(eVD​/(nVT​)−1))

Words: 410 Articles: 5
Diode OurBigBook.com
For a p-n junction at fixed temperature, the Shockley diode equation models its electric current as
ID​=IS​(expnVT​VD​​−1),VT​=qkB​T​.
(3)
Here IS​>0 is the diode saturation current, n>0 the diode ideality factor, VT​ the thermal voltage, kB​ the Boltzmann constant, and q>0 the elementary charge.[ref]
For an original model example, choose IS​=1nA, n=2, and T=300K. Using kB​=1.380649×10−23J/K and q=1.602176634×10−19C gives VT​=25.8520mV. Then VD​=0.600V gives ID​=0.109591mA, whereas VD​=0.800V gives ID​=5.24450mA. These are predictions of the declared model. There is no universal turn-on electric potential difference: solving the Shockley diode equation for the value needed at a chosen electric current gives
VD​=nVT​ln(1+IS​ID​​),ID​>−IS​.
(4)
At ID​≫IS​, increasing VD​ by 0.100V multiplies the electric current by approximately e0.100/(nVT​)=6.91772. At VD​=−0.300V the same model gives ID​=−0.996979nA. Its reverse branch approaches −IS​; it cannot describe diode reverse breakdown.
A constructed extension adds internal series electrical resistance Rs​ to a junction whose electric potential difference is Vj​. Applying the Kirchhoff cycle law gives
VD​=Vj​+ID​Rs​=nVT​ln(1+IS​ID​​)+ID​Rs​.
(5)
For Rs​=20Ω and the same IS​,n,T, sustaining ID​=5.24450mA needs VD​=0.904890V: 0.800V across the junction plus 0.104890V across its internal electrical resistance. The derivative
dID​dVD​​=ID​+IS​nVT​​+Rs​
(6)
shows why the current-voltage characteristic becomes nearly a straight line when the internal series electrical resistance dominates. This is still a fixed-temperature model; self-heating can change IS​, n and VT​. Real diodes also have leakage and charge-storage effects omitted here.[ref]

Diode minority-carrier diffusion current (IS​=eAni2​[Dn​/(Ln​NA​)+Dp​/(Lp​ND​)])

Words: 83
Shockley diode equation OurBigBook.com
For a long, nondegenerate, ideal p-n junction under low injection, the diode saturation current is set by minority carriers supplied from the neutral regions. Their equilibrium densities are np0​=ni2​/NA​ and pn0​=ni2​/ND​. Solving the steady diffusion and recombination equations gives IS​=eA(Dn​np0​/Ln​+Dp​pn0​/Lp​), where A is junction area, Dn​,Dp​ are diffusion coefficients, and Ln​,Lp​ are diffusion lengths. Reverse bias suppresses opposite majority-carrier injection exponentially while collecting this minority supply. Thus IS​ is approximately bias independent before breakdown, but depends strongly on temperature through ni2​ and on transport, doping, and geometry.

Extracting a semiconductor band gap from diode saturation current
Words: 66
Diode saturation current OurBigBook.com
In a diffusion-dominated p-n junction, Is​=C(T)ni2​ with a transport prefactor determined by minority-carrier diffusion and dopant densities. Combining this with the intrinsic carrier concentration gives, for fixed gap and effective masses,
logC(T)T3Is​​=constant−kB​TEg​​.
(7)
The slope against 1/T is −Eg​/kB​. A measured diode ideality factor helps identify the transport regime: generation or recombination current can have a different dependence on ni​, so its activation slope cannot automatically be interpreted with the diffusion formula.

Diode reverse breakdown

Diode OurBigBook.com
A sufficiently large reverse electric potential difference can produce a rapidly increasing reverse electric current. Both the ideal diode model and the unextended Shockley diode equation omit this behavior.[ref]

Diode characteristic measurement

Words: 229
Diode OurBigBook.com
The New Jersey Institute of Technology laboratory uses a silicon 1N4148 diode. For its forward current-voltage characteristic, the supply operates in current-source mode; a benchtop voltmeter independently reads the diode electric potential difference. Small electric current steps resolve the steep branch. For reverse measurements, a sensitive ammeter sits in series; the handout suggests a 10–100kΩ series resistor. Reversing the applied polarity supplies the comparison. Meter placement must avoid counting the voltmeter's own electric current, and the zero reading may have an offset. The same diode is then measured with an Agilent U2722A source measure unit for graphical comparison.[ref]
The prescribed analysis uses a logarithmic scale for forward electric current to infer IS​ and n from the straight region. Large-electric current departures can indicate series electrical resistance. The handout cautions that the accessible range may not determine it precisely; meter loading also matters. This is a measurement procedure, without a published set of device readings.[ref]
The reason for the logarithmic scale follows directly from the Shockley diode equation. If ID​≫IS​ and series electrical resistance is negligible,
ln(I0​ID​​)≈ln(I0​IS​​)+nVT​VD​​,
(8)
where I0​>0 is a fixed reference electric current making the logarithm dimensionless. The slope is 1/(nVT​), so extracting n needs the junction temperature. Fitting only an appropriate interval matters: a straight-looking subset cannot establish the model at all electric currents.

A rectifier converts an alternating input into a unidirectional output. Diode orientation selects which direction of electric current is transmitted.[ref]

Voltage multiplier

Words: 41
Rectifier OurBigBook.com
An electrical circuit that uses diodes and capacitors to produce an output electric potential difference larger in magnitude than the input peak. The attainable output depends on the circuit arrangement, electric current drawn by the load, capacitance and input frequency; an ideal unloaded result does not specify the output under load.

Half-wave rectifier (vL​(t)=max(0,vS​(t)))

Words: 299
Rectifier OurBigBook.com
A half-wave rectifier with one diode and a resistor load passes one half of each input cycle.[ref]
For an original ideal example, let an ideal voltage source supply the sinusoid vS​(t)=Vp​sin(ωt), with Vp​=5V and angular frequency ω>0. Connect its positive reference terminal to the diode anode, the diode cathode to the upper terminal of a load resistor with electrical resistance RL​=1kΩ, and the lower terminal to the source return. Let vL​ be the upper-minus-lower load electric potential difference, and iL​ the downward load electric current. Assume the ideal diode model, zero source electrical resistance, and no filter capacitor, inductor or switching delay.
The Kirchhoff cycle law gives vS​=VD​+vL​, and Ohm's law gives vL​=RL​iL​. If vS​>0, the blocking assumption would give VD​=vS​>0, contradicting the ideal diode model, so the diode conducts with VD​=0. If vS​<0, conduction would give iL​=vS​/RL​<0, also forbidden, so the diode blocks. At the crossings both values vanish. Thus
vL​(t)=max{0,Vp​sin(ωt)},iL​(t)=RL​vL​(t)​.
(9)
The peak load electric current is 5mA. The output is unidirectional but still varies in time, reaching zero throughout every negative half-cycle. Over a period of a function 2π/ω, write the wave phase as θ=ωt. Its average value of a function and root mean square follow from two integrals:
vL​=2π1​∫0π​Vp​sinθdθ=πVp​​=1.59155V,vL,rms​=(2π1​∫0π​Vp2​sin2θdθ)1/2=2Vp​​=2.500V.
(10)
Consequently the average load power is vL,rms2​/RL​=6.25mW, not vL2​/RL​. The ideal diode has zero loss; the resistor converts supplied energy into Joule heating. The same switching argument predicts vL​=min(0,vS​) when the diode is reversed. Directional selection changes the waveform and its average value of a function; it does not by itself produce a constant output.

Light-emitting diode

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Diode OurBigBook.com
A light-emitting diode is a semiconductor diode producing electroluminescence under electric current. Forward bias injects electrons and electron holes; radiative electron-hole recombination emits photons. A double heterostructure uses band offsets to retain both charge carriers in an active layer. A sufficiently thin layer is a quantum well.[ref]
The optical and electrical questions are different: photon energy sets a color scale, while light-emitting diode efficiency determines how much supplied energy escapes as light. The blue light-emitting diode made compact white light-emitting diodes and full-color displays practical. A modulated light-emitting diode can also supply the optical signal in a chopped-light lock-in experiment.

Blue light-emitting diode

Words: 626 Articles: 1
Light-emitting diode OurBigBook.com
Blue transitions motivate wide-bandgap semiconductors, but a large band gap alone cannot guarantee efficient emission. Gallium nitride has a direct band gap; indium gallium nitride composition tunes the transition energy.[ref]
For an emitted photon, with frequency ν and vacuum wavelength λ,
Eγ​=hν=λhc​,λ=Eγ​hc​,
(11)
where h is the Planck constant and c the vacuum speed of light. Multiplying energy by wavelength gives hc=1239.841984eVnm. Thus chosen wavelengths 450nm and 630nm correspond to 2.75520eV and 1.96800eV: blue requires more energy per photon than red. A stipulated transition energy 3.40eV instead gives 364.659nm, in the ultraviolet. These are conversions, not measured emission lines.
For near-edge emission, Eγ​≈Eg​ estimates the photon energy from the emitting material's band gap. Quantum well confinement or impurity transitions can change it. The 1994 blue light-emitting diode used zinc-doped indium gallium nitride, emitting below its near-edge transition.[ref]
The measured forward terminal electric potential difference Vf​ is also not fixed by Eg​/q, where q is the elementary charge. It depends on electric current, temperature, contacts and series electrical resistance. Even the simple Shockley diode equation with series electrical resistance has Vf​=Vj​+IRs​, whereas an optical transition does not acquire an extra energy qIRs​ merely because the contact drop increases. Consequently, extracting a band gap from one terminal-voltage reading is not justified.
GaN blue LED development
Words: 439
Blue light-emitting diode OurBigBook.com
Isamu Akasaki chose metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy and sapphire, which tolerated hot Ammonia. Large lattice mismatch hindered film growth. In 1985, Hiroshi Amano and Isamu Akasaki's group developed an aluminium nitride epitaxial buffer layer deposited before hotter gallium nitride growth. The buffer supplies initial growth sites; growing islands join into a continuous film. It improves growth without making the lattices identical. Isamu Akasaki separately credits Shuji Nakamura's 1991 gallium nitride buffer.[ref]
The 1986 growth paper reports a vertical metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy reactor, source gases mixed just before delivery to slanted sapphire, and subsequent gallium nitride growth over aluminium nitride. Surface microscopy, X-ray diffraction and photoluminescence tested different aspects of the result. Buffered and unbuffered growth supplied the comparison. Its reported preparation conditions should not be replaced by one universal buffer temperature: the later lecture's account of the first low-temperature trial and the paper's parameter study describe different stages of development.[ref]
A magnesium acceptor impurity in gallium nitride accepts a valence band electron, leaving a mobile electron hole. Hydrogen passivation of magnesium acceptors in gallium nitride suppresses this activity. Post-growth activation restores existing impurities' electrical activity; ionization of active acceptor impurities supplies mobile electron holes. Adding magnesium alone is insufficient.[ref]
In 1989, Hiroshi Amano, Masahiro Kito, Kazumasa Hiramatsu and Isamu Akasaki obtained p-type semiconductor conduction in magnesium-doped gallium nitride using low-energy electron beam irradiation. Hiroshi Amano recalls initially resistive samples, an unreliable hot-probe test, then Masahiro Kito's Hall effect confirmation. A junction irradiated in an M-shaped region emitted in that pattern. Treatment, carrier-sign measurement and spatial emission supplied different evidence. Earlier zinc-doped samples brightened under irradiation without becoming p-type semiconductors: brightness alone did not prove the carrier sign.[ref]
Shuji Nakamura, Takashi Mukai, Masayuki Senoh and Naruhito Iwasa's 1992 thermal-activation paper established another route using annealing in nitrogen. Their companion study compared already conducting films heated in nitrogen with films heated in Ammonia: the latter became highly resistive again. Its hydrogen-complex explanation connected this atmosphere dependence to acceptor impurity passivation. These are thermal treatment and atmosphere comparisons, distinct from the earlier electron beam intervention; neither observation alone images an individual hydrogen complex.[ref][ref]
Shuji Nakamura's two-flow metalorganic chemical vapor deposition reactor, gallium nitride buffer, thermal activation and improved indium gallium nitride growth enabled bright double heterostructure devices, followed by thinner quantum well devices.[ref]
The original 1994 paper by Shuji Nakamura, Takashi Mukai and Masayuki Senoh describes a sapphire/gallium nitride-buffer device with zinc-doped indium gallium nitride emission and aluminium gallium nitride confinement. After nitrogen annealing, etching exposed the n-side for a separate contact. At room temperature, varied forward electric currents gave emission spectra and optical-output curves alongside a current-voltage characteristic. At 20mA: 1.5mW output, 450nm peak wavelength, 3.6V terminal electric potential difference. The peak stayed nearly fixed across the current series. The paper omits a complete calibrated collection apparatus; comparisons with earlier devices change several preparation details.[ref]

Efficiency has several denominators. Specify a steady electric current I>0, positive terminal electric potential difference Vf​, and a simplified narrow emission spectrum with photon energy Eγ​. Assume at most one radiative photon per injected electron and electron hole pair. Let ηinj​ be the fraction of the electrical pair-supply rate I/q reaching the active layer, ηrad​ the fraction of those pairs recombining radiatively, and ηext​ the fraction of internally emitted photons that escape. Then counting the successive events gives
N˙active​=ηinj​qI​,N˙internal​=ηrad​N˙active​,N˙out​=ηext​N˙internal​.
(12)
Define internal quantum efficiency here conditionally on pairs reaching the active layer: ηIQE​=ηrad​. The internal photon yield per electrical pair is instead ηinj​ηIQE​. Stating this convention matters when another definition folds injection into internal quantum efficiency. The external quantum efficiency and wall-plug efficiency are
ηEQE​=I/qN˙out​​=ηinj​ηIQE​ηext​,ηWPE​=IVf​Popt​​=ηEQE​qVf​Eγ​​,Popt​=N˙out​Eγ​.
(13)
These are photon-count and energy-flow identities for the declared model. For a broad spectrum, replace Eγ​ by the mean escaping photon energy, weighted by photon number, when computing optical power.
A stipulated example chooses I=20mA, Vf​=3.20V, λ=450nm, ηinj​=0.90, ηIQE​=0.80 and ηext​=0.50. For every 100 electrical pairs, 90 reach the active layer, 72 emit internally, and 36 photons escape. Thus ηEQE​=0.36, not 0.80. Using q=1.602176634×10−19C gives
I/qN˙out​Popt​ηWPE​​=1.24830×1017s−1,=4.49389×1016s−1,=19.8375mW,IVf​=64.0mW,=0.309960.​
(14)
The dimensional analysis is transparent: A/C=s−1, J/s=W, and CV=J. The optical and electrical efficiencies differ because Eγ​/q=2.75520V differs from the chosen Vf​.
The factors suggest different improvements. Better confinement can reduce injection leakage; suppressing nonradiative recombination raises the radiative fraction; improving light extraction efficiency helps already-emitted photons escape. A photon trapped by total internal reflection has already passed the radiative step and can still be lost through absorption. Improving extraction therefore need not change the internal radiative fraction.
Shuji Nakamura's lecture cautions that why indium gallium nitride emits efficiently despite many defects was not completely settled in that account.[ref]
As an independent consistency check on the 1994 reported values, treating its broad spectrum as monochromatic at the 450nm peak gives
ηEQE​≈(0.020A)(hc/(450nm))(1.5×10−3W)q​=0.02722.
(15)
This agrees at the quoted precision with the reported 2.7%. Its optical/electrical power ratio is instead 1.5mW/(20mA×3.6V)=2.0833%. The first estimate uses a peak in place of a photon-number-weighted mean, so agreement is a consistency check rather than an exact reanalysis of the measured spectrum.

An operational amplifier is a differential electronic amplifier whose unloaded voltage is modeled in its linear regime by vo​=A(s)(v+​−v−​). Lock-in amplifier

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Electronic amplifier OurBigBook.com
A lock-in amplifier measures the component of an input signal synchronized with a reference at a chosen frequency. It multiplies the input by a reference sinusoid, then uses a low-pass filter to retain the slowly varying product. Two references in phase quadrature recover both amplitude and phase difference. A shared timing source keeps the relative wave phase stable: this is coherent detection.[ref]
The useful trick is to move the wanted frequency to zero before averaging. An electronic amplifier alone enlarges both the wanted signal and unwanted noise; a lock-in amplifier instead selects a component by its timing. A photodiode's electric current can first be converted to an electric potential difference, so the same calculation can measure weak modulated light. The chopped-light lock-in experiment makes this selection tangible.

phase-sensitive detection correlates an input with a synchronized reference and filters the product. Sinusoidal quadrature references recover both signal amplitude and relative phase. Narrow detection bandwidth rejects incoherent noise but cannot reject a background coherent at the same frequency; changing the integration time also changes settling and tracking speed.[ref]

X=T2​∫0T​s(t)cosωtdt,Y=−T2​∫0T​s(t)sinωtdt.
(21)
These integrals average the products with dimensionless references 2cosωt and −2sinωt; X and Y have the input's units. The minus sign makes positive ϕ give positive Y. The trigonometric functions give
2s(t)cosωt−2s(t)sinωt​=Acosϕ+Acos(2ωt+ϕ),=Asinϕ−Asin(2ωt+ϕ).​
(22)
The oscillating terms have zero integral over the stated interval, proving X=Acosϕ and Y=Asinϕ. Their orthogonality turns an oscillating signal into two constant coordinates.
Represent those coordinates as a vector, or as the complex number Z=X+iY. Its modulus and complex argument recover the peak amplitude and phase difference:
R=X2+Y2​=A,ϕ=atan2(Y,X)(mod2π),R>0.
(23)
Here atan2(Y,X) selects the angle with the correct signs of both coordinates, rather than applying the arctangent to Y/X and losing the quadrant. When X=Y=0, the amplitude is zero and the phase difference is undefined. When ϕ=π/2, X=0 despite a nonzero signal; measuring Y prevents this blind spot. Rotating both references by a fixed angle rotates the coordinate vector but preserves R.
The factors of two above deliberately recover peak amplitude. The SR830 instead reports the selected sinusoidal component in root mean square units: in a calibrated, zero-offset display, Rrms​=R/2​. For R=0.4V this is 0.282843V, while the peak-to-peak span of that component is 0.8V. Display normalization, reference sign, gain and angle units must be checked for the particular instrument.[ref]

The University of California, Berkeley guide LLS - Measuring the Light Signal from a Diode, in Experimental Setup and Experiments X–XI, documents an experiment using a red light-emitting diode amid room-light background. An optical chopper, controlled by an SR540, periodically interrupts its light. A PIN-10DP photodiode sends electric current to an SR570 preamplifier, which converts it to an electric potential difference for an SR760 spectrum analyzer and an SR830 lock-in amplifier. The SR540 supplies the external reference. Preparation includes aligning the photodiode and its shielding cone and choosing gain to avoid overload. One comparison first searches for the source frequency without the chopper reference, then checks against that external reference; switching off the LED tests the candidate spectral peak. The measurement procedure varies chopper frequency and preamplifier filtering, then records repeated lock-in readings with selected averaging settings. These are prescribed observations to make, not published numerical results.[ref]
The guide notes nearly triangular chopping because slit and emitter sizes are comparable. Its interpretation requires detector conversion, preamplifier gain and waveform geometry to infer optical power from the selected component.[ref]
The inference is therefore specific: synchronized electric potential difference supports the presence of a modulated optical component at the reference frequency. It does not by itself give total emitted optical power. The photodiode's spectral responsivity, collected fraction of the light, and conversion from the measured Fourier coefficient to the chopped waveform must enter that calibration. The finite-window lock-in response also explains why a frequency-search reading can drift when the reference is not synchronized. An LED-off comparison tests background at the same timing; it cannot guarantee that every synchronized disturbance disappears when the desired source is present. Overload before multiplication destroys information that later averaging cannot restore.

Passive sign convention (pabsorbed​=VI)

Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
The passive sign convention defines terminal electric potential difference V=ϕ(A)−ϕ(B) and positive electric current entering at A. Then VI is absorbed electrical power: positive means the component receives energy, negative means it supplies energy. Reversing both reference directions leaves the product unchanged. For a positive electrical resistance obeying Ohm's law, both V and I reverse together and Joule heating remains I2R≥0.

Electrical impedance (Z(ω)=V/I)

Words: 3k Articles: 18
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
Electrical impedance is the ratio of terminal electric potential difference and electric current phasors at one specified positive angular frequency ω. For an electrical circuit modeled as a linear time-invariant system, use the sinusoidal steady state after any decaying transient has settled. With the passive sign convention, positive electric current enters the terminal assigned positive electric potential difference. Define peak complex amplitudes by
v(t)=Re(Veiωt),i(t)=Re(Ieiωt),Z(ω)=IV​,I=0.
(31)
The physical v(t) and i(t) are real; the complex numbers encode their amplitudes and wave phases. The unit of electrical impedance is the ohm, 1Ω=1V/A. Both phasors may instead use root mean square magnitudes, with the same ratio Z. A nonlinear diode can generate additional frequencies; a single Z(ω) then does not describe the whole response.
Write the electrical impedance in Cartesian and polar forms as
Z=R+iX=∣Z∣eiϕ,R=ReZ,X=ImZ,∣Z∣=R2+X2​,ϕ=argZ=argV−argI.
(32)
Here R is the resistive real part, X the signed electrical reactance, and ϕ the voltage-minus-current phase difference, defined modulo a full turn. The Pythagorean theorem gives the modulus from a right triangle in the complex plane. The complex argument gives the rotation from the current phasor to the voltage phasor. Thus Vrms​=∣Z∣Irms​, while negative ϕ means electric current leads terminal electric potential difference. For R>0, ϕ=arctan(X/R) lies between −π/2 and π/2; outside that case, use the quadrant of the complex number rather than a bare inverse tangent. The geometric magnitude and phase difference are the two pieces of the AC relation.[ref]
Multiplication by Z acts on phasors, not on instantaneous physical signals. For example, when i(t)=I0​cosωt,
v(t)=I0​(Rcosωt−Xsinωt).
(33)
The second term is in phase quadrature with electric current; it cannot be represented by pointwise multiplication v(t)=Zi(t) when X=0. This is the useful compression: one complex multiplication replaces separate amplitude and phase difference calculations, while the real part restores the physical signal.
An ideal resistor, inductor and capacitor have ZR​=R, ZL​=iωL and ZC​=1/(iωC). Their electrical impedances add in a series RLC circuit, giving Z=R+i(ωL−1/(ωC)). The current amplitude is V0​/∣Z∣, so cancellation of the imaginary parts explains the resonant series RLC response. The component-law derivation and opposite complex exponential convention are in reactance phase convention.

A lossless intermediate section of positive real characteristic impedance ZM​ matches unequal real exterior characteristic impedances ZL​,ZR​ when ZM2​=ZL​ZR​ and its propagation wave phase is an odd multiple of π/2. The length is an odd quarter of the internal wavelength. This principle also applies to the characteristic impedance of a stretched string.
For a uniform intermediate string of length l, put δ=kM​l. Continuity of displacement and transverse force gives the displacement reflection coefficient
r=(ZL​+ZR​)cosδ−i(ZM​+ZL​ZR​/ZM​)sinδ(ZL​−ZR​)cosδ+i(ZM​−ZL​ZR​/ZM​)sinδ​.

At real positive mechanical impedances, the denominator never vanishes. Its numerator vanishes only if (ZL​−ZR​)cosδ=0 and (ZM2​−ZL​ZR​)sinδ=0. Thus unequal exterior strings require the quarter-wave condition. Equal exterior strings with a different middle string instead transmit perfectly at integer half-wavelengths; if all three mechanical impedances agree, every frequency is matched.

Electrical impedance OurBigBook.com
Consider a stipulated series circuit containing an ideal resistor of electrical resistance R=100Ω and an ideal capacitor of capacitance C=1μF. The same electric current passes through both. Their terminal electric potential differences add by Kirchhoff's voltage law, so
V=VR​+VC​=RI+iωCI​,Z=R−ωCi​.
(35)
A quick derivation uses i=CdvC​/dt: taking the derivative of the complex exponential multiplies the capacitor voltage phasor by iω, hence VC​=I/(iωC). Dimensionally, 1/(ωC) has units s/F=V/A=Ω, matching R.
At frequency f=1000Hz, the angular frequency is ω=2πf. The signed capacitive electrical reactance, modulus and complex argument of the total electrical impedance are
XC​=−159.154943Ω,∣Z∣=187.963549Ω,ϕ=−57.858092∘.
(36)
Apply Vrms​=1.00V across the complete series circuit. Its root mean square electric current is
Irms​=187.963549Ω1.00V​=5.320180mA.
(37)
With voltage as the zero-phase reference, the current phasor has complex argument +57.858092∘: electric current leads. The phasor drops have moduli VR,rms​=0.532018V and VC,rms​=0.846733V; these add as complex numbers, not as positive magnitudes. Their squared magnitudes sum to (1.00V)2.
The mean absorbed power uses the root mean square values:
P=Vrms​Irms​cosϕ=RIrms2​=2.830432mW,cosϕ=∣Z∣R​=0.532018.
(38)
The ideal capacitor has zero cycle-averaged absorbed power; all the mean absorbed power becomes Joule heating in the resistor.[ref] To see why the phase factor appears, average p(t)=v(t)i(t) over a full cycle with v(t)=2​Vrms​cosωt and i(t)=2​Irms​cos(ωt−ϕ). The cosine addition formula reduces the average to Vrms​Irms​cosϕ; the term at 2ω averages to zero. Independently, pC​=d(CvC2​/2)/dt, and the capacitor energy returns to its starting value after each cycle.
At fixed applied Vrms​, the limit ω→0+ gives ∣Z∣→∞, ϕ→−π/2 and Irms​→0: the ideal capacitor blocks steady electric current. The limit ω→∞ gives Z→R, ϕ→0 and Irms​→Vrms​/R. These are limits of the ideal lumped electrical circuit; unwanted lead inductance and component losses can invalidate that model at high frequency. At ωRC=1, the equal legs of the impedance right triangle give ∣Z∣=2​R and ϕ=−π/4 without numerical evaluation. Measuring both the magnitude and the sign of the phase difference distinguishes this capacitor response from an equally large positive electrical reactance.

Leipzig University's laboratory handout Measurements with an oscilloscope, experiment E 3e, uses a function generator, a two-channel oscilloscope, a known resistor and a capacitor. Figure 5 places the capacitor above the resistor, with a common return below the resistor. Channel 1 measures the applied terminal electric potential difference v1​; channel 2 measures vR​. The handout asks for peak-to-peak values and relative timing, then comparison of measured and calculated electrical impedances with R=3kΩ, C=0.47μF at 100 and 300Hz. It also asks students to check the oscilloscope time base against a digitally counted generator frequency. These are apparatus and procedural specifications, not reported measured results.[ref]
For this arrangement, Ohm's law gives i(t)=vR​(t)/R if probe loading and the sensing resistor's electrical reactance are negligible. Record both voltage magnitudes with the same convention: peak, peak-to-peak, or root mean square. After the transient settles, compare matched rising zero crossings t1​ of v1​ and tR​ of vR​, with period T=1/f. Then
∣Z∣=RVR​V1​​,Δt=tR​−t1​,ϕ=T2πΔt​,Z=∣Z∣(cosϕ+isinϕ).
(39)
The recovered electrical impedance includes the known resistor. For a separate unknown component in series with that resistor, subtract R from the inferred total electrical impedance. A current crossing earlier than the applied voltage crossing gives Δt<0, hence negative ϕ. For the stipulated series RC impedance example at 1000Hz, this predicts Δt=−0.160717ms; it is a calculated timing, not a lab observation. Timing supplies the complex argument that an amplitude ratio alone cannot recover.
As additional measurement controls, first feed the same sinusoid to both channels to check relative delay and polarity; then replace the reactive chain with a known resistor, expecting nearly zero phase difference. Keep both probe returns at the common return shown in figure 5. A reversed voltage polarity adds half a turn to its inferred wave phase. Match crossings with the same slope and choose −T/2<Δt≤T/2; adjacent cycles otherwise change ϕ by a full turn. A sweep continuous in frequency helps track that branch. These controls test the signed inference rather than assuming that the scope's delay readout has the desired sign.
Measure the loaded terminal electric potential difference on channel 1 at every frequency. The generator's output impedance can change the applied magnitude; its front-panel setting is not the measured terminal value. The generator's internal electrical impedance is outside the terminal ratio above, while the known sensing resistor is inside it. Probe loading, finite timing resolution, component tolerances and distorted waveforms limit the inference. A repeat at lower drive amplitude tests whether one linear electrical impedance still fits. Electrical reactance bench measurement develops these loading and reference-direction issues further.

Electrical reactance (X=ImZ)

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Electrical impedance OurBigBook.com
Electrical reactance X is the signed imaginary part of electrical impedance Z=R+iX, measured in ohms. It describes the part of the terminal electric potential difference in phase quadrature with the electric current in a sinusoidal steady state. In the eiωt convention, an ideal inductor has XL​=ωL>0 and an ideal capacitor has XC​=−1/(ωC)<0 for ω>0. A large ∣X∣ reduces electric current at fixed applied voltage, but an ideal purely reactive component returns the energy it receives over each cycle. This is why electrical reactance and electrical resistance have the same units yet describe different physical behavior. [ref].
In a series RLC circuit, electrical impedances add because the same electric current passes through every component. For ideal positive inductance L, capacitance C, and total electrical resistance RΣ​>0,
X(ω)=ωL−ωC1​,∣Z∣=RΣ2​+X2​,Irms​=∣Z∣Vrms​​,ϕ=arctanRΣ​X​.
(40)
Here ϕ is voltage wave phase minus current wave phase. Below ω0​=1/LC​, X<0 and electric current leads terminal voltage; above it, X>0 and electric current lags. At ω0​, the two signed electrical reactances cancel, leaving Z=RΣ​ and the maximum electric current at fixed terminal voltage. This is the resonant series RLC response. Electrical resistance does not cancel: the toy circuit gives f0​=ω0​/(2π)=1591.55Hz and Irms​=9.091mA there. These numbers follow directly from the stipulated component values. [ref].
Cancellation concerns terminal voltage, not the disappearance of stored energy. In the toy circuit at resonance, the individual inductor and capacitor voltages are each 0.9091V in root mean square magnitude, with opposite wave phases, while their sum is zero. Their peak stored magnetic energy and capacitor energy are each 0.8264μJ, attained at different times. With smaller positive RΣ​, either component voltage can exceed the applied voltage. This ability to select a frequency while sustaining internal energy exchange connects electrical reactance to tuning and frequency response.
For an ideal inductor or capacitor, the absorbed instantaneous power equals the rate of change of stored energy:
pL​=vL​i=dtd​(21​Li2),pC​=vC​i=dtd​(21​CvC2​).
(41)
Positive power stores energy; negative power returns it. Over a periodic steady state, each stored energy returns to its initial value, so its cycle-averaged absorbed power is zero. An ideal resistor instead has pR​=Ri2≥0, transferring energy into Joule heating. More generally, the average terminal power of this series RLC circuit is
p​=Vrms​Irms​cosϕ=Irms2​RΣ​.
(42)
Zero average power in an ideal reactive component does not imply zero instantaneous power, zero electric current, or zero stored energy. Real coils and capacitors have losses, so zero ideal reactive loss is a model assumption rather than a claim about every component. [ref].

The complex amplitudes here use peak magnitudes; both can instead use root mean square magnitudes without changing their ratio. Choose positive electric current entering the terminal assigned positive voltage, so p=vi is absorbed power. For an ideal linear inductor and capacitor, their terminal laws vL​=Ldi/dt and iC​=CdvC​/dt give

Taking i(t)=I0​cosωt as a reference gives vL​(t)=−ωLI0​sinωt and vC​(t)=I0​sinωt/(ωC) for the sinusoidal response. Thus inductor voltage leads electric current by π/2, while capacitor voltage lags electric current by π/2. A constant offset or a free transient is outside this single-frequency representation. [ref].
With the alternative e−iωt convention, the same real signals use conjugated complex amplitudes and ZL​=−iωL, ZC​=+i/(ωC). Their physical leads and lags stay the same; the sign of ImZ changes. Also, some textbooks call the positive magnitude 1/(ωC) the capacitive reactance and write the series expression as XL​−∣XC​∣. This article consistently uses signed XC​=−1/(ωC) and hence X=XL​+XC​. Electrical reactance OurBigBook.com
The motivating observation is a pair of sinusoids on an oscilloscope: changing frequency changes both their relative amplitudes and their phase difference. Gary Tuttle's EE 201 laboratory uses resistor voltage as the current-phase reference, compares predictions with readings at several frequencies, and explicitly asks students to measure component values and account for coil electrical resistance. The following bench arrangement applies that method to a series RLC circuit; its component values and illustrated traces are our own toy example. [ref].
Connect a low-voltage sine generator to a series chain ending in a known sensing resistor Rs​ at the common return. Use a resistor whose unwanted inductance is negligible over the chosen frequency range. An oscilloscope displays voltage against time: channel A reads the loaded voltage across the whole chain, and channel B reads the voltage vs​ across Rs​. Both channel ground connections and the generator return meet at that same node. Ordinary bench oscilloscope grounds are electrically common; attaching one to an intermediate circuit node would change the circuit. A separate floating component voltage needs a suitable differential measurement, rather than moving a ground clip. [ref].
After the free transient decays, record frequency f, period T=1/f, both voltage amplitudes, and matched rising zero-crossing times tA​,tB​. Check that the traces are sinusoidal. Define Δt=tB​−tA​ on the branch ∣Δt∣<T/2. With negligible probe loading and negligible sensing-resistor electrical reactance, vs​=Rs​i, so channel B is the electric current reference, and in the reactance phase convention
Irms​=Rs​Vs,rms​​,∣Zchain​∣=Irms​VA,rms​​,ϕ=T2πΔt​,Xchain​=∣Zchain​∣sinϕ,Rchain​=∣Zchain​∣cosϕ.
(45)
A later current crossing gives Δt>0, hence positive electrical reactance; an earlier crossing gives negative electrical reactance. Use the same amplitude convention for both channels. An amplitude-only ratio recovers ∣Z∣, so it cannot distinguish the two signs: timing supplies the missing information. The formulas follow from Z=∣Z∣eiϕ and the chosen terminal orientation.
Begin with a known resistor replacing the reactive chain: its expected phase difference is approximately zero, testing channel polarity and relative delay. Measure the same signal with both channels to establish the instrumental delay baseline, then exchange probes to check that a phase offset does not belong to one channel. Next test an inductor and a capacitor separately with Rs​: after subtracting Rs​ from the inferred real part, expect approximately X/f=2πL and fX=−1/(2πC), respectively. Finally combine L,C,R,Rs​ and sweep through the predicted resonance. These are proposed controls and consequences of the model, not reported observations.
For the toy series RLC circuit, the prediction at 500Hz is X=−286.894Ω, ∣Z∣=307.259Ω, ϕ=−69.02∘, and Vs,rms​=32.55mV. At 5000Hz, X=+282.328Ω and ϕ=+68.71∘. Near 1591.55Hz the model predicts zero phase difference and Vs,rms​=90.91mV. Keep actual loaded VA,rms​ fixed or normalize by it at each frequency; the generator's display alone does not establish that voltage. The 10Ω sensing resistor is part of the 110Ω total and therefore changes the predicted peak electric current.
Real components add unintended electrical impedance: coil wire has electrical resistance, nearby turns add capacitance, and capacitor leads add inductance. These effects can produce a component's own resonance, beyond which the ideal ωL or −1/(ωC) approximation fails. Work in a range where that approximation is adequate, measure coil wire electrical resistance, and compare the inferred Rchain​ with the sensing resistor, intended resistor, and component losses. A measured nonzero real part is evidence of loss in the assembly, not negative or positive electrical reactance becoming heat. [ref]; [ref].
The probes also add electrical resistance and capacitance to the measured nodes; their loading becomes more important as frequency increases. Use compensated probes with known input electrical impedance and short ground connections, and repeat with a smaller drive voltage to test whether the inferred X depends on amplitude. [ref]. Record actual voltage and phase readings separately from calculated predictions, with component tolerances and timing uncertainty. A phase error δϕ alone produces approximately δX=∣Z∣cosϕδϕ, so near zero electrical reactance, a small delay can imitate a small residual X. Agreement within stated uncertainties tests the model; the smooth toy curves establish no experimental accuracy.

Electric battery

Words: 2k Articles: 20
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An electric battery converts the available chemical Gibbs free energy of one or more galvanic cells into electrical work delivered to an electrical load. The reacting materials are a finite reservoir: a battery can sustain a terminal electric potential difference while discharging, but cannot supply energy indefinitely. Unlike a capacitor, whose capacitor energy resides in an electric field, a battery chiefly stores its available energy in the chemical state of its materials. The detailed half-reactions and apparatus of a Daniell cell explain this conversion at the electrode level.
During discharge, electrons move through metallic wires from the negative anode, through the electrical load, to the positive cathode; external conventional current points the other way. Inside the battery, ions carry electric current through the electrolyte, and redox chemical reactions connect ionic transport to electronic transport at the electrodes. The same electron does not make a lap through both wire and electrolyte. Electric charge conservation closes the circuit; changing chemical composition supplies the energy. See galvanic cell for the two transport paths and electrolyte for how oppositely moving ions contribute to one net electric current.
The source's electromotive force E measures its driving work per unit electric charge, in volts; the loaded terminal electric potential difference VL​ measures the electrical work per unit electric charge delivered outside the battery. They agree in an ideal lossless source, or approximately near open circuit, but generally differ during discharge.[ref]
In the ideal fixed-voltage model used in fixed-voltage capacitor energy balance, a battery maintains a prescribed terminal electric potential difference while electric charge flows to or from the capacitor. This is a constraint for that calculation, not an inexhaustible reservoir. The fixed-voltage capacitor energy balance also accounts for electrical energy returned to the source; an actual cell can accept sustained charging only if its chemistry and operating conditions permit it.

Battery internal resistance (VL​=E−Ir)

Words: 185
Electric battery OurBigBook.com
A useful short-interval approximation replaces a battery by an ideal electromotive force E in series with a positive internal electrical resistance r. This is the Thévenin terminal response with open-circuit voltage E and Thévenin resistance r. The model describes the terminals without asserting that there is a separate physical resistor hidden inside the cell. Both E and r can change with composition, temperature, electric current and history.[ref]
For a resistive electrical load R>0, take I>0 to mean discharge: conventional current leaves the positive terminal. Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law give
E−Ir−IR=0,I=R+rE​,VL​=IR=E−Ir.
(46)
For the stipulated E=3V, r=1Ω, R=4Ω,
I=0.6A,Ir=0.6V,VL​=2.4V.
(47)
An open-circuit voltage of 3V therefore does not promise 3V at this electrical load. Increasing the load electrical resistance reduces electric current and brings VL​ closer to E, as in Thévenin load response.
The signed relation also explains charging within this model. If an external source drives electric current into the positive terminal, I<0 and VL​=E+∣I∣r. The terminal electric potential difference then exceeds E. This algebra is not evidence that every battery is rechargeable.[ref]

Battery load power and efficiency (PL​=E2R/(R+r)2)

Words: 277
Electric battery OurBigBook.com
In the constant-parameter battery internal resistance model, the source's available electrical power splits between the electrical load and internal dissipation:
EI=PL​VL​I​​+Pint​I2r​​,PL​=(R+r)2E2R​,Pint​=(R+r)2E2r​.
(48)
The stipulated 3V, 1Ω, 4Ω calculation gives PL​=1.44W, Pint​=0.36W, and EI=1.80W. A resistive electrical load converts its share to Joule heating; another electrical load might convert some of it to mechanical work or light. The source term is available electrical work per time, not a complete cell heat budget: reaction entropy can also matter.
Define the delivery efficiency relative to the source's available electrical work, rather than to all chemical energy or to a complete charging cycle:
η=EIPL​​=EVL​​=R+rR​.
(49)
Here η=0.80. The largest load power occurs at R=r: since (R+r)2≥4Rr,
PL​≤4rE2​,PL​​R=r​=2.25W,η​R=r​=21​.
(50)
Thus maximum load power and maximum delivery efficiency ask different questions. As R→∞, VL​→E and η→1, but I→0 and PL​→0: a high nearly unloaded voltage supplies almost no power. As R→0, the model gives VL​→0, PL​→0 and internal power tending to E2/r. Real high-current operation can invalidate constant r and E; the mathematical maximum does not establish a permissible operating point for an actual battery.

Finite battery charge reservoir (Qdelivered​=∫Idt)

Words: 201
Electric battery OurBigBook.com
A battery's charge reservoir means a finite amount of electric charge can pass through the external electrical circuit before its usable chemical state is depleted. It does not mean a large net electric charge is sitting inside the casing. For one net cell chemical reaction transferring n electrons per reaction event, an ideal reaction inventory obeys
Qdelivered​=∫0t​I(t′)dt′=nFξ,WL​=∫0t​VL​(t′)I(t′)dt′,
(51)
where F is the Faraday constant and ξ the extent of reaction in moles, assuming all the electric current serves that reaction. At fixed temperature and pressure, its reversible electromotive force obeys Δr​G=−nFE: a decrease in Gibbs free energy provides the maximum reversible electrical work per mole. The electromotive force also depends on composition; the Daniell cell illustrates this with thermodynamic activity.[ref]
As an original finite-reservoir exercise, stipulate usable Qmax​=360C and hold the preceding 3V, 1Ω, 4Ω parameters constant until an abrupt cutoff. Then t=Qmax​/I=600s, available electrical work is EQmax​=1080J, load work is VL​Qmax​=864J, and internal dissipation is 216J. This explicitly finite idealization predicts ten minutes, not an experimentally measured runtime. Real accessible charge depends on discharge conditions and the chosen terminal-voltage cutoff. Charge alone is also not an energy: converting it to delivered work requires the terminal electric potential difference throughout discharge.

Battery voltage measurement experiment

Words: 270
Electric battery OurBigBook.com
The institutional handout Measurement of Emf Using a Potentiometer, Oklahoma Christian University laboratory (Experimental Activity: calibration procedure, measuring a test cell, and measuring internal resistance of a cell) compares unloaded and loaded battery readings. Its apparatus uses a slidewire potentiometer, calibrated resistance coils, a reference cell, a galvanometer, a nominal 1.5V flashlight cell, a voltmeter, and a switched variable resistor branch with an ammeter. Calibration uses the reference cell's tagged electromotive force; zero galvanometer deflection establishes a null measurement. With the load branch open, the null reading draws no test-cell electric current. The protocol compares newer and older cells using both instruments, then records simultaneous loaded terminal electric potential difference and electric current. It prescribes brief measurements, opening the load switch between readings, and periodic calibration rechecks. These are documented procedures, not run data.[ref]
For the battery internal resistance model, VL​=E−rI. The handout's analysis estimates electromotive force from the intercept and r from the negative slope, then compares the intercept with the independent null reading.[ref]
Additional replication controls are to repeat the open-load reading after the sweep, return to an earlier load setting to detect drift, and record temperature, elapsed time, instrument resolution and measurement error. Include ammeter and contact electrical resistance in the external path; allow for voltmeter loading if a voltmeter replaces the null instrument. The Thévenin measurement experiment gives the corresponding meter-loading correction. Curvature or time-dependent readings can reject the constant-r approximation, but a terminal curve alone does not identify which internal transport or electrode process caused the deviation. These extra controls and interpretations are model-based extensions, not reported outcomes of the handout.

RL circuit (LdI/dt+RI=V)

Words: 522 Articles: 2
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An RL circuit combines electrical resistance R and self-inductance L. In the series model, the same electric current I flows through both components. An ideal battery maintains terminal electric potential difference V; the drops in the direction of positive electric current obey Ohm's law and the inductor relation:
vR​=RI,vL​=LdtdI​,V=vR​+vL​.
(52)
This is Kirchhoff's voltage law with the inductor's terminal drop, rather than its oppositely signed induced electromotive force. For constant R>0, L>0, and V, the first-order linear differential equation has solution
I(t)=I∞​+(I(0)−I∞​)e−t/τ,I∞​=RV​,τ=RL​.
(53)
The time constant τ measures exponential decay of the difference from the final electric current. [ref].
For a stipulated example, take electrical resistance R=2Ω, self-inductance L=0.5H, terminal electric potential difference V=6V, and initial electric current I(0)=0. Then
τ=0.25s,I∞​=3A,I(t)=(3A)(1−e−t/(0.25s)).
(54)
With t measured numerically in seconds, this is I(t)=3(1−e−4t) in amperes. At one time constant,
I(τ)=3(1−e−1)A≈1.89636A,
(55)
and the terminal electric potential difference drops are
vR​(τ)=6(1−e−1)V≈3.79272V,vL​(τ)=6e−1V≈2.20728V.
(56)
Their sum is exactly 6V. At t=0+, the inductor takes the entire terminal electric potential difference while the electric current is still zero. At steady electric current, the inductor's terminal drop is zero and the entire drop is across the electrical resistance.
The final magnetic energy stored by the inductor is U∞​=LI∞2​/2=2.25J. At one time constant, the electric current has reached about 63.21% of its final value, but its magnetic energy has reached only about 39.96%:
U(τ)=21​LI(τ)2=2.25(1−e−1)2J≈0.899047J.
(57)
This difference follows from the square of electric current in the inductor's magnetic energy.
For release, take t=0 at the start of a separate experiment with initial electric current 3A. Remove the battery from the model while maintaining a closed path through the same electrical resistance and inductor. Then
LdtdI​+RI=0,I(t)=(3A)e−t/(0.25s).
(58)
Now vL​=−vR​: the induced electromotive force supports the continuing positive electric current as its magnitude decreases. This closed-loop model describes exponential decay, not opening the sole path and imposing an instantaneous jump to zero electric current. The inductor's magnetic energy and the power of Joule heating are
U(t)=(2.25J)e−2t/τ,PR​(t)=RI(t)2=(18W)e−2t/τ,dtdU​=−PR​.
(59)
Their time constant is τ/2=0.125s. The total energy dissipated by Joule heating is exactly the initial magnetic energy:
∫0∞​PR​(t)dt=(18W)2τ​=2.25J.
(60)
The second diagram in inductor shows this energy transfer. A finite closed path lets us predict both how long the electric current persists and how much energy becomes heat. [ref].

Inductor branch shunted by a resistor (τ=L/(2R))

Words: 64
RL circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal source V feeds a series resistance 2R, followed by parallel branches R+L and 2R. The Thévenin equivalent seen by the inductor has voltage V/2 and resistance R+(2R∥2R)=2R. From zero initial current, the inductor current is V(1−e−t/τ)/(4R), the other branch current is V(1+e−t/τ)/(8R), and the source current is V(3−e−t/τ)/(8R). Kirchhoff's current law holds at every time, and the final stored magnetic energy is LV2/(32R2).

Periodically switched RL circuit (Imax​=(V/R)/(1+e−RΔt/L))

Words: 70
RL circuit OurBigBook.com
An RL circuit alternating for equal intervals Δt between zero drive and constant drive V has a unique attracting periodic electric current when R,L,Δt>0. Write s=e−RΔt/L and J=V/R. Sampling just before each zero-drive interval gives the recurrence relation In+1​=s2In​+J(1−s). Subtracting its fixed point yields In​−J/(1+s)=s2n[I0​−J/(1+s)]. Thus the limiting upper and lower electric currents are J/(1+s) and sJ/(1+s); convergence is geometric. This gives a simple exact ripple estimate for a periodically driven inductor.

RLC circuit

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An RLC circuit combines electrical resistance R, inductance L, and capacitance C. The capacitor stores energy in its electric field; the inductor stores energy in its magnetic field. Their exchange can produce an oscillation, while Joule heating removes energy. A series RLC circuit gives a particularly clear example: changing R turns ringing into a direct return to equilibrium, and changing L or C tunes a resonance.
These circuits connect two useful viewpoints. In time, they describe how stored energy is released after switching. In frequency, they select a range of signals: the resonant series RLC response explains radio tuning and simple filters. The same mathematics describes a damped harmonic oscillator, so insight about mechanical ringing transfers directly to an electrical circuit. [ref]; [ref].

Driven RLC branch with a parallel shunt resistor (Umax​/Wdiss​=ω0​L/(4πR))

Words: 51
RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal sinusoidal voltage source drives a series R,L,C branch and a separate resistor R in parallel. At the series resonance, the reactive stored energy is LV02​/(2R2), while both resistors together dissipate 2πV02​/(ω0​R) per cycle. Counting only the series resistor overestimates the stored-energy-to-dissipation ratio by a factor of two.

Parallel RLC circuit (Y(ω))

RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
An ideal resistor, inductor and capacitor connected across the same voltage have admittance Y=1/R+i(ωC−1/(ωL)) in the eiωt convention. At ω0​=1/LC​ the reactive branch currents cancel, giving minimum source current V0​/R and maximum impedance R. This differs from a lossy series coil placed across a capacitor.

Free parallel RLC voltage decay (V′′+V′/(RC)+V/(LC)=0)

Parallel RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
With no external current, Kirchhoff's current law is CV˙+V/R+IL​=0, and LI˙L​=V. Differentiating gives the title equation. For 4R2>L/C, its real solutions are Ae−t/(2RC)cos(ωd​t+ϕ) with ωd2​=1/(LC)−1/(4R2C2). The original current balance fixes the compatible initial inductor current. A single complex exponential represents a physical voltage through its real part; general complex solutions require both conjugate characteristic roots.

Parallel RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
When Rs​ is in series with a parallel RLC circuit, the ratio of parallel-network voltage to voltage across Rs​ is its impedance divided by Rs​. Its peak is R/Rs​, and its phase passes from +π/2 through zero to −π/2 as angular frequency rises through 1/LC​. This is not the transfer ratio relative to the total input voltage, which includes the additional series voltage drop and has peak R/(R+Rs​). Identifying voltage endpoints is necessary before using the voltage divider formula.

Parallel RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
For the ratio of resistor-current amplitude to total-current amplitude to exceed 1/2​, ∣ωC−1/(ωL)∣<1/R. The exact positive endpoint difference is Δω=1/(RC) and the quality factor is Q=RC/L​. Greater shunt resistance means weaker dissipation, unlike increasing a series resistance.

Series RLC circuit (Lq′′+Rq′+q/C=V(t))

Words: 1k Articles: 6
RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
In a series RLC circuit, the same electric current i=q′ flows through the resistor with electrical resistance R, the inductor, and the capacitor. Choose q as the signed electric charge on the capacitor plate into which positive i flows. With terminal drops measured in that direction, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives
vR​=Ri,vL​=Li′,vC​=q/C,Lq′′+Rq′+q/C=V(t).
(61)
Here V(t) is the applied electric potential difference; assume constant L>0, C>0, and R>0. With the applied source set to zero and the loop kept closed, the free response satisfies
q′′+2αq′+ω02​q=0,α=2LR​,ω0​=LC​1​.
(62)
The angular frequency ω0​ is the value for lossless free oscillation; α is the decay parameter. The three possibilities are underdamped RLC response for α<ω0​, critically damped RLC response for α=ω0​, and overdamped RLC response for α>ω0​. [ref].
For a fair comparison, start each circuit with the same electric charge q(0)=q0​ and zero electric current q′(0)=0. Set τ=ω0​t and a=α/ω0​; then x=q/q0​ obeys d2x/dτ2+2adx/dτ+x=0. The plot compares a=0.5,1,2. These dimensionless curves apply to any L,C after rescaling time and electric charge.
The stored energy is the sum of magnetic energy and capacitor energy:
E=21​Li2+2Cq2​.
(63)
Differentiating and using the circuit equation gives the complete power balance,
E′=i(Li′+Cq​)=V(t)i−Ri2.
(64)
In the free response, E′=−Ri2≤0: Joule heating accounts exactly for the lost energy. For the plotted initial conditions, E(0)=q02​/(2C) and E/E(0)=x2+(dx/dτ)2. Since every free solution tends to zero for R>0,
∫0∞​Ri(t)2dt=E(0).
(65)
In the lossless limit R=0, energy stays constant and shuttles between the capacitor and inductor. Thus an oscillation of electric charge and a decrease of total energy are compatible statements.
The analogy with a damped harmonic oscillator is exact within these ideal models: electric charge corresponds to displacement, electric current to velocity, inductance to mass, 1/C to spring constant, and R to the coefficient of a resisting force proportional to velocity. The two stored energy terms play the roles of kinetic energy and elastic potential energy. [ref].
Differentiating the driven equation also gives Li′′+Ri′+i/C=V′. When using this equation to solve for electric current, retain the original constraint Li′(0)+Ri(0)+q(0)/C=V(0): the initial electric charge fixes the initial rate of change of electric current.

Series RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
For series resistance R, inductance L and capacitance C, with output measured across the inductor, the eiωt transfer function is HL​=iωL/[R+i(ωL−1/(ωC))]. At current resonance ω0​=1/LC​ its modulus is ω0​L/R=Q. Large and oppositely phased inductor and capacitor voltages nearly cancel in the loop sum. This is voltage magnification in a passive circuit, not power gain. The maximum of ∣HL​∣ need not occur exactly at the current-resonance frequency.

Displacement and current bandwidths of a series RLC circuit

Words: 89
Series RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
Write ω02​=1/(LC) and γ=R/L for a series RLC circuit. The squared charge response has denominator D=(ω02​−ω2)2+γ2ω2. Its nonzero resonance peak occurs at ωr2​=ω02​−γ2/2. The two squared half-height frequencies, when both exist, are
ω±2​=ω02​−2γ2​±γω02​−4γ2​​.
(66)
Their difference in angular frequencies is only approximately γ at large quality factor. The electric current instead has ∣I∣2=∣V∣2/[R2+(ωL−1/(ωC))2]. Its exact half-power frequencies satisfy ∣ωL−1/(ωC)∣=R, whose positive roots differ by R/L, independently of capacitance. Thus an exact capacitance-independent bandwidth applies to current or resistor-voltage output; capacitor-voltage output is a low-pass response with a possible resonant peak.

Resonant series RLC response (Iamp​(ω0​)=V0​/R)

Words: 360
Series RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
Drive a series RLC circuit with electric potential difference V(t)=V0​cos(ωt), where V0​>0 and ω>0. After the free transient decays, the electric current has the same angular frequency as the source:
iss​(t)=Iamp​cos(ωt−ϕ),Iamp​(ω)=R2+(ωL−1/(ωC))2​V0​​,tanϕ=RωL−1/(ωC)​,−2π​<ϕ<2π​.
(67)
For fixed positive R,L,C,V0​, the electric current amplitude is largest exactly at ω=ω0​=1/LC​. The two electrical reactance contributions cancel there, leaving only the drop from electrical resistance. In particular,
iss​(t)=RV0​​cos(ω0​t),qss​(t)=Rω0​V0​​sin(ω0​t).
(68)
Every solution approaches this periodic response because its difference from the displayed solution is a decaying free response. The peak remains at ω0​ even for an overdamped RLC response; free ringing is not required for a maximum of driven electric current. [ref].
For example, stipulate L=10mH, C=1μF, R=20Ω, and V0​=1V. Then ω0​=104s−1, f0​=ω0​/(2π)≈1591.55Hz, and the peak electric current amplitude is 50mA. Holding the source amplitude fixed is essential when comparing responses at different frequencies.
Three frequencies must be distinguished. The free underdamped RLC response rings at ωd​=ω02​−α2​. Driven electric current peaks at ω0​. Driven electric charge has amplitude
qamp​(ω)=ωIamp​(ω)​=(ω02​−ω2)2+4α2ω2​V0​/L​,
(69)
whose peak occurs at ω02​−2α2​ only if α<ω0​/2​. Otherwise it decreases from its zero-frequency limit CV0​, with no positive-frequency peak. The different peak locations follow because electric current is the time derivative of electric charge, multiplying a sinusoidal amplitude by ω. The limiting responses are Iamp​∼V0​Cω as ω→0+ and Iamp​∼V0​/(Lω) as ω→∞.
The Q factor measures selectivity:
Q=RLω0​​=2αω0​​.
(70)
The average Joule heating power is RIamp2​/2. Its half-maximum angular frequencies and their separation are exactly
ω±​=ω02​+α2​±α,Δω=ω+​−ω−​=2α=LR​=Qω0​​.
(71)
These follow by setting ∣ωL−1/(ωC)∣=R. In the numerical example, Q=5 and Δω=2000s−1. Reducing R makes a taller, narrower electric current peak; varying C tunes the selected frequency. Measuring the drop vR​=Ri gives a band-pass filter that suppresses very low and very high frequencies while passing a range near resonance. This is useful for selecting a radio signal, though the range must be broad enough to pass its modulation. [ref].

Words: 94
Series RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
An overdamped RLC response is a free series RLC circuit response with R>2L/C​, equivalently α>ω0​. Put β=α2−ω02​​. The distinct negative characteristic roots are r±​=−α±β, so the general electric charge is
q(t)=Aer+​t+Ber−​t,i(t)=q′(t).
(72)
For initial conditions q(0)=q0​, i(0)=0,
q(t)=q0​e−αt(cosh(βt)+βα​sinh(βt)),i(t)=−βq0​ω02​​e−αtsinh(βt).
(73)
For q0​>0, this electric charge decreases to zero without reversing sign. In the dimensionless example ω0​=1, α=2, the characteristic roots are −2±3​≈−0.268,−3.732. The slow term dominates late times. Stronger damping can therefore make the final return slower: for α≫ω0​, r+​∼−ω02​/(2α)=−1/(RC). Nonoscillation alone does not imply a fast response, and monotonicity here uses the specified initial conditions.

Series RLC circuit OurBigBook.com
A critically damped RLC response is the boundary between underdamped RLC response and overdamped RLC response. The free series RLC circuit has a repeated characteristic root −ω0​, with general solution
q(t)=(A+Bt)e−ω0​t.
(74)
For initial conditions q(0)=q0​, i(0)=0,
q(t)=q0​(1+ω0​t)e−ω0​t,i(t)=−q0​ω02​te−ω0​t.
(75)
In the plotted normalization, q(1)=2/e≈0.735759 and i(1)=−1/e≈−0.367879. The electric charge returns without ringing; the polynomial factor 1+ω0​t matters, so a single exponential function does not give the whole response.
For fixed L,C and these initial conditions, critical damping avoids ringing while giving a faster asymptotic return than any larger R: the overdamped RLC response has a root closer to zero. This makes critical damping a useful tuning target for settling after switching. An MIT laboratory exercise makes the distinction observable by asking students to compare all three cases with L=47mH and C=47nF. Those values give Rcrit​=2L/C​=2000Ω and ω0​≈21276.6s−1. [ref].

The electric charge first crosses zero at t=4π/(33​)≈2.41840 and reaches its first negative extremum at t=2π/3​≈3.62760, where q/q0​=−e−π/3​≈−0.163034.

Integrated circuit

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Electrical circuit OurBigBook.com
An integrated circuit combines interconnected electrical circuit elements in a fabricated structure. A monolithic integrated circuit forms its elements in or on one piece of semiconductor, rather than merely putting separately manufactured components into one enclosure. Transistors supply control in electronic amplifiers; resistors and capacitors can supply bias and timing. Jack St. Clair Kilby's patent describes making such functions from a common semiconductor body with compatible fabrication steps.[ref]
The useful change is to fabricate connections and functions together. Shrinking an enclosure still leaves individual parts to position and join. Integration makes their relative arrangement part of a repeatable fabrication pattern. The distinction is functional as well as geometric: one small piece can implement a whole electrical circuit, while its external terminals expose only the connections needed by its surroundings.
