Words: 115
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
A monolithic integrated circuit has its circuit elements fabricated in or on one semiconductor die. Their connections are essential: an unconnected collection of transistors does not implement the intended electrical circuit.
An original ideal example separates function from fabrication. Connect two resistors, R1​=10kΩ above R2​=20kΩ, in a series circuit across an ideal 3V voltage source. With no load electric current drawn from their meeting point, Ohm's law and the Kirchhoff cycle law give
I=R1​+R2​3V​=0.1mA,Vout​=IR2​=2V.
(78)
These equations apply to either a discrete circuit or an idealized monolithic integrated circuit realizing those same electrical resistances. Integration changes construction; the electrical circuit equations still determine the output. A real load, unwanted capacitance or finite resistor tolerance changes the ideal calculation. Manufacturing many functions together also couples their fate: a fatal defect can discard an entire semiconductor die, motivating the Poisson defect yield model.

Kilby integrated circuit demonstration

Words: 175
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
In his 2000 lecture, Jack St. Clair Kilby describes an August 1958 comparison circuit made from separate silicon elements. Resistors were cut and etched; capacitors came from diffused, metallized semiconductor wafers. It tested whether semiconductor elements could perform all the required functions, but was still a discrete circuit. For the September prototype he used already diffused germanium material with contacts, cut into bars, and hand-applied wax masks to define a transistor and a distributed resistor-capacitor region. Applying supply power produced an oscillation.[ref]
An inspected eyewitness interview describes the germanium on a microscope slide with protruding wires; changing its connections changed the oscilloscope display from a straight line to a sinusoid. This supplied a qualitative connected/disconnected comparison, not a calibrated record of amplitude, loading or repeatability.[ref]
The inference was feasibility: integrated semiconductor elements could cooperate as an operating electrical circuit. The hand-wired germanium prototype did not yet supply the deposited integrated circuit interconnects of Robert Noyce's silicon design. Nor does a working prototype establish manufacturing yield or long-term reliability.

Planar process

Words: 70
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
The planar process fabricates semiconductor devices from a common surface while retaining a protective oxide over the exposed ends of their p-n junctions. Jean Hoerni's patent describes selective openings in silicon dioxide for semiconductor doping and contacts, with oxide left over the p-n junctions. Protection and access are designed together; the surface is not simply stripped after fabrication. This was a distinct enabling contribution to the monolithic integrated circuit.[ref]

Integrated circuit interconnect

Words: 79
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
An integrated circuit interconnect is a conducting path joining circuit regions. In Robert Noyce's patent, deposited metal strips cross retained oxide on silicon; selected openings permit contact to the semiconductor while oxide prevents unwanted contact across p-n junctions. Figs. 3–5 combine detection, filtering and electronic amplifier functions using a transistor in one structure. The key is both connectivity and insulation: a metal path must touch its intended terminals while crossing other regions without shorting them.[ref]

Semiconductor wafer

Words: 60 Articles: 1
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
A thin piece of semiconductor processed to form devices or integrated circuits, often many semiconductor dies together. Dividing wafer area by die area gives an ideal count before edge losses and spaces used to separate semiconductor dies.

Semiconductor die

Words: 30
Semiconductor wafer OurBigBook.com
A piece of semiconductor carrying a fabricated device or integrated circuit, ordinarily separated from a larger semiconductor wafer. One package can contain multiple semiconductor dies; the package boundary and the semiconductor die boundary are different concepts.

Poisson defect yield (Y=e−DA)

Words: 551 Articles: 1
Integrated circuit OurBigBook.com
Consider a deliberately simplified model: fatal defects form a spatially uniform Poisson point process with intensity D per unit area. A semiconductor die of area A works exactly when it contains no fatal defect. Its defect count N has a Poisson distribution with expected value DA, hence its probability of working, called its yield, is
Y=Pr(N=0)=0!(DA)0​e−DA=e−DA.
(79)
The product DA is dimensionless. The formula concerns fatal defects, not every visible imperfection. Spatial uniformity, independent defect counts in disjoint areas, and failure from even one fatal defect are model assumptions. Clustering, shared processing failures, repairable regions and defects that affect only some functions can invalidate them. This is a chosen probability model, not historical yield data.
Choose D=0.005mm−2. For semiconductor die areas 25, 100 and 200mm2, the model gives Y=e−0.125=0.882497, e−0.5=0.606531 and e−1=0.367879. Doubling the area squares the yield: Y(2A)=Y(A)2. This follows either from the exponential function or by splitting the larger area into two disjoint parts and using independence. More functions on one semiconductor die can save assembly while making the no-defect requirement harder to satisfy.

Integrated circuit cost per good die (Cgood​=Cw​/(Ng​Y))

Words: 329
Poisson defect yield OurBigBook.com
Let a circular semiconductor wafer have diameter d and processed cost Cw​. For square semiconductor dies of area A, ignoring all edge losses gives the ideal gross count N0​=πd2/(4A). For illustration adopt the geometric edge approximation
Ng​≈4Aπd2​−2A​πd​,E[G]≈Ng​e−DA,Cgood​≈Ng​e−DACw​​.
(80)
Here G is the good-die count. The correction scales as wafer perimeter divided by die side length: only a boundary strip can lose partially fitting squares. Its coefficient is an approximation depending on layout; the expression is not an exact packing theorem and is useful only when A​≪d. Counts from it need not be integers. Actual layouts, edge exclusion and separation lanes determine an integer gross count. The expected value of G follows by linearity of expectation; independence between semiconductor dies is not required for that step if each has the same yield.
For the original example d=200mm, A=100mm2, D=0.005mm−2 and Cw​=1000 cost units, N0​=314.159 and Ng​≈269.730. The predicted good count is 163.600 per wafer, and the processed cost is 6.11248 units per good die. This is total processed cost divided by expected output, appropriate to a large repeated batch; it is not the expected value of a single-wafer random ratio Cw​/G, which is undefined when G=0. Test, packaging, design and equipment costs are excluded.
A hypothetical test readout makes the inference explicit. Suppose 600 of 1000 tested semiconductor dies, each of area 100mm2, pass a specified functional test. These are invented counts for calculation, not reported measurements. The pass fraction is Y=0.600; within the Poisson defect yield assumptions it implies
D=−AlnY​=0.00510826mm−2.
(81)
If pass indicators are independent random variables with common success probability Y, their sum has a binomial distribution. The fitted standard deviation of the pass fraction is 0.6(1−0.6)/1000​=0.01549. A test readout estimates pass probability for its tested functions and conditions; it cannot alone establish spatially independent defects, detect every latent failure or distinguish fabrication losses from a faulty test. The logarithm only translates the observed fraction into a defect intensity after those additional assumptions are adopted.
